tagline.text: The heart of Aklan, carried on by black-faced dancers and piña looms

image.credit: Benedict Esber / CC BY 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The capital of Aklan province in northwestern Panay Island, home to the Ati-Atihan Festival, often called the mother of all Philippine festivals. With UNESCO-recognized piña weaving workshops and a 220-hectare mangrove forest, it's a great place to spend a day on the way to Boracay.

Kalibo is the capital of Aklan province, sitting at the mouth where the Aklan River meets the Sibuyan Sea in northwestern Panay. With a population of about 90,000, it's the province's largest city and commercial hub, widely known as the gateway to Boracay thanks to Kalibo International Airport, which has direct flights from Korea. Many travelers board a bus to Caticlan straight from the airport, but even a single day here lets you experience the old culture and festival traditions of the Visayas region up close.

Kalibo's history reaches back before the Spanish era. Legend holds that ten datus (chieftains) who crossed over from Borneo bought land on Panay from the native Ati people, and that painting their faces with soot and dancing to celebrate this purchase became the root of the Ati-Atihan Festival. The city took shape when a Spanish encomienda was established here in
, and during the Philippine Revolution, on
March 23, 1897
, 19 Aklanon patriots who had joined the revolutionary society Katipunan were executed here. The Aklan Freedom Shrine, honoring them, is designated a National Historical Shrine.

Another heritage that defines Kalibo is piña, cloth woven from pineapple leaf fiber. Thin, translucent, and lustrous, this fabric is used as the finest material for the barong Tagalog, the Philippines' traditional formal wear, and Aklan's hand-loom piña weaving technique was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in
. At family workshops around town, you can watch the whole process firsthand, from scraping out the fiber to mounting it on the loom and weaving it thread by thread.

Rather than expecting grand ruins or beaches, come here to see local living culture — festivals, crafts, and the riverside mangrove forest. Adding a half-day or an overnight stay on your way to or from Boracay makes your trip richer, and during the January festival, Kalibo becomes a destination in its own right.
A festival honoring the Santo Niño (Child Jesus), reaching its peak every year on the
third Sunday of January

, when tribal groups with faces and bodies painted black parade through the streets to the beat of drums. What makes it special is that it's a participatory festival — tourists can join in too, dancing and shouting "Hala Bira!"
The cathedral of the Diocese of Kalibo, dedicated to St. John the Baptist. Built on its current site in the
early 1800s
, it has been restored several times after major fires and earthquake damage. During the festival, it fills with pilgrims coming to venerate the image of the Santo Niño.

At old family workshops like the Dela Cruz House of Piña in New Buswang, you can watch the entire process of scraping pineapple leaves for fiber and weaving it on a loom. Small items like handkerchiefs or scarves also make good souvenirs.
About 220 hectares of mangrove forest revived by planting on tidal flats, considered one of the leading success stories in Southeast Asia. Walk the roughly
1.1km
bamboo boardwalk, and the sea opens up at the far end of the forest.
The Aklan provincial museum, housed in a renovated old schoolhouse built in
beside Pastrana Park. Its displays of pre-Spanish artifacts, Ati-Atihan costumes, and piña textiles offer a complete overview of Aklan culture.

A monument and grave site honoring the 19 martyrs executed during the revolutionary period. Nineteen steps, each dedicated to one of the martyrs, make even a brief visit a reminder of Kalibo's modern history.

An Aklan delicacy of woodworm-like mollusks that live inside mangrove wood, eaten raw dipped in vinegar and seasoning. Soft and briny like an oyster, it can usually be sampled around Bakhawan Eco-Park.
A tiered waterfall in Tangalan, about
30–40 minutes
from downtown by car, with several pools good for a cooling swim.

If visiting during the festival, it's best to devote all of Day 2 to the street parades and cathedral Mass. On the third Saturday of January, tribal groups compete, and the grand procession is held on Sunday.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly daily from Manila to Kalibo International Airport (KLO), taking about
1 hour
. One-way fares run around
, varying widely by season.
Direct flights from Incheon to Kalibo also operate, taking about
4 hours 30 minutes
. Airlines and flight frequency change seasonally, so check the latest schedule.
The airport is close to downtown, about
10–15 minutes
away by tricycle.
Ceres buses run frequently from Iloilo City to Kalibo, taking about
4–5 hours
, for around
. Vans are a bit faster.
From Roxas City it's about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by bus or van, and from Caticlan (the Boracay jetty) about
1 hour 30 minutes
, for around
If you're bringing a car, take the RoRo sea highway running Batangas–Calapan–Roxas (Oriental Mindoro)–Caticlan. It involves two ferry transfers and takes about
12–16 hours
from Manila, so it suits travelers who want a leisurely road trip.
Tricycles are the main way to get around town. A shared ride costs about
per person, while a chartered ride to Bakhawan Eco-Park costs about
one way.
The New Buswang tricycle terminal is near Kalibo's public market, making it convenient for reaching the workshops and eco-park. For Jawili Falls, a half-day chartered vehicle is most convenient.
December–May
is the relatively clear, dry season, good for exploring downtown and walking the eco-park.
March–May
especially is the hottest stretch, with midday temperatures reaching
, so it's best to split outdoor plans between morning and late afternoon.
June–November
is the rainy wet season, and when a typhoon crosses Panay, flights and road traffic to Caticlan can come to a halt.
The high point of a Kalibo trip is the Ati-Atihan Festival. Events typically run from the
second week of January
, closing with the grand procession and Mass on the
third Sunday of January
. Lodging sells out months ahead during this period, and rates double or triple, so book early. During Holy Week (the week before Easter), a quieter church procession is also held.

Lodging clusters around the town center (Poblacion), home to the cathedral and Pastrana Park, and along the road to the airport. Clean business hotels run about
a night, while simple pensions and guesthouses run about
. If you're catching an early flight or arriving late, lodging near the airport is convenient, and during the festival you should stay downtown so you don't miss the parades.

Aklanon cuisine makes generous use of coconut. Binakol, a clear soup of chicken simmered with coconut water in a bamboo tube or pot, and inubaran, chicken simmered with banana pith in coconut milk, are the signature local dishes. Crab, shrimp, and dried fish from the Aklan River mouth are also fresh and cheap, and if you're feeling adventurous, try tamilok, the mangrove woodworm. In the evening, sampling grilled skewers and banana cue at barbecue stalls around the market is a quintessential Kalibo experience.
Flights to Kalibo for Boracay are often much cheaper than flying into Caticlan. Spending a night in Kalibo and exploring downtown eases travel fatigue and adds another destination to your trip.
At the Ati-Atihan Festival, many people will paint your face with soot or paint. Wear clothes you don't mind ruining, bring a waterproof bag, and put your phone in a zip bag.
Museo it Akean mainly operates on weekdays, so if visiting on a weekend, check ahead whether it's open.
Bakhawan Eco-Park is cooler after
than at midday, and the sea view at the end of the boardwalk is more beautiful at high tide.

Genuine piña fabric is expensive, with fine fibers that shimmer softly when held up to the light. Cheaper products are often blended with polyester or banana fiber, so it's safer to buy directly from a workshop.
There are plenty of bank ATMs downtown, but workshops, stalls, and tricycles are cash-only, so carry plenty of small bills.
For trips to and from Boracay, many counters at the airport sell tickets straight through to Caticlan. Compare fares and departure times before choosing one.

During the festival, huge crowds bring more pickpocketing and lost belongings. Leave valuables at your lodging, and agree on a meeting point with your group in advance in case you're separated in the middle of the parade.
Lodging and airfare spike sharply during the festival and year-end holidays. Book at least 2–3 months ahead.
The bamboo boardwalk at Bakhawan Eco-Park is slippery after rain, and some sections may be worn, so walk carefully. Bring insect repellent too.
For raw dishes like tamilok, check the hygiene conditions, and if you have a sensitive stomach, try just a small taste.
During the wet season and typhoon period, flights can be cancelled and roads can flood. Check weather advisories before you leave.
At the cathedral, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and avoid taking photos during Mass.
